say: Welcome—this workshop keeps us in Copilot Chat on the web, with five prompts spread across three stages. The opening cards show the route: practise your first three prompts, review three sample files, then prepare an email you can check and edit.

There are two ways into that first stage, depending on whether you can see Work IQ. Neither route is a lesser exercise, and everyone comes together for the file-based work; today we're practising useful requests and careful judgement, not trying to produce identical answers.
welcome.ask: Would organising your day or preparing a checked service update be more useful to you right now?
welcome.watch: Use the three stage cards to outline the session; mention both routes before anyone assumes Work IQ is required for participation.

say: These cards ask us to use authorised work information, keep personal details about the public out of prompts and check sources before acting. The fourth card also explains why neighbours may get different results: their work information isn't the same as yours.

Keep any real calendar, email or Teams content private while you practise. We can discuss whether an answer was supported without reading confidential messages to the group, and we shouldn't treat a different response as a mistake simply because it doesn't match someone else's.
needs.ask: How could you describe a source-checking problem without exposing the private message itself?
needs.watch: Pause on Expect different results; don't encourage side-by-side sharing of real work calendars or inboxes.

say: Open the web address shown in the mock and look at the top left of your own Copilot Chat. Choose Track A if you can see Work IQ, which takes you through your calendar, emails and Teams messages for prompts one to three.

If that button isn't there, choose Track B for three public-service examples that need no work data. The two choice cards are clickable, and both routes rejoin at Checkpoint 1, so if you're uncertain, select B and keep learning rather than waiting on setup.
track.ask: Can you see the Work IQ button in your own chat, and which track will you choose?
track.watch: Let learners select their own track; use the correct branch while presenting and explain that A and B steps are alternatives, not six consecutive tasks.

say: This setup step belongs to Track A; Track B goes directly into its public-service examples. Follow the highlighted web address, sign in with your work account and check the Work IQ button at the top left.

For the next three Track A prompts, keep it on as the page instructs so you can work with your own information. There's no prompt to send on this screen; if you can't find the button, switch to Track B instead of spending the whole activity troubleshooting.
setup.ask: Is Work IQ visible and on, or would Track B let you start practising now?
setup.watch: Present this step only on Track A; confirm account and button privately, without asking for sign-in details.

say: Track A begins with your day: the animation sends a request for meetings and appointments in time order, with brief context and possible focus gaps. Try it in a new chat and then open the calendar source to compare the response with your actual schedule.

A gap in that response is a suggestion to inspect, not a guarantee that you're free. Check the meeting times and whether the descriptions really match the entries before using the answer to plan your work, and keep those entries off the shared screen.
t1do.ask: Does one suggested focus gap match your calendar, and is the meeting context supported by its entry?
t1do.watch: Keep the presentation on Track A; wait for learners to check their own calendar instead of inventing a sample schedule.

say: Stay in the same Track A chat so this request follows the calendar exercise. We're asking about emails and Teams messages from the last two working days, focused on public services, and explicitly asking Copilot not to invent unstated deadlines.

Open the citations behind items labelled for response, action or attention. If the filter returns nothing relevant, use the displayed suggestion to remove the public-services filter; the purpose is to find checkable work items, not to force an answer about services you don't handle.
t2do.ask: Does one listed action have a real source, and is any deadline actually stated there?
t2do.watch: Check that Track A learners stay in the same chat; offer the filter adjustment without asking them to expose message contents.

say: Now Track A turns the items from that same conversation into a plan, rather than starting a new search. Send the prompt and compare the four groups: Handle first, Complete today, Waiting for someone else and Monitor for an update.

Check the explanation and source for each priority, including whether any stated deadline was retained accurately. Separating your own actions from dependencies can make the plan easier to use, but the order still needs your judgement about what actually matters today.
t3do.ask: Which item belongs under Waiting for someone else rather than Complete today, and what source supports that?
t3do.watch: Do not advance through the Track B alternatives as extra Track A tasks; pause for source checks before the shared checkpoint.

say: Track B starts without calendar or work-message access, using the public-service example in the prompt. Ask for a short, simple explanation of generative AI, then send the follow-up that changes the audience to a resident who has never used AI.

Compare those two answers rather than looking for a single model response on the screen. Notice which jargon disappeared and whether the public-service example became clearer; changing the audience is a practical way to improve an explanation while still checking its accuracy.
a1do.ask: What wording changed when the audience shifted from a government team member to a resident?
a1do.watch: Present this on Track B only; make sure learners send both the initial prompt and its audience-changing follow-up.

say: Keep the same Track B chat and paste the rough notes about Saturday's online-service interruption. The prompt provides the important facts: eight until twelve, telephone support remains, submitted applications are unaffected and the work is for a system upgrade.

After reading the public notice, request the shorter website-banner version and compare both with those notes. Brevity helps only if the essential facts survive, so check that the rewrite hasn't added a promise or removed the alternative way residents can get help.
a2do.ask: Which fact must stay visible even in the shorter website banner?
a2do.watch: Have learners compare against the supplied fictional notes, especially the hours and telephone alternative; do not turn the draft into a real public notice.

say: The last Track B exercise asks for options to improve access to online services without removing phone or in-person support. Send the prompt and inspect the table's benefits and considerations for residents facing internet, accessibility, language or confidence barriers.

Use the follow-up to explore which options could fit a small pilot, then read the reasoning critically. The point is to surface alternatives and trade-offs for people to decide, not to treat a suggested pilot as an approved service change.
a3do.ask: Which pilot option appears to preserve non-digital support, and what consideration still needs a human decision?
a3do.watch: Keep all discussion tied to the fictional access challenge; emphasise that Copilot's reasoning is input to a decision, not the decision.

say: Let's regroup here: Track A has worked through day, messages and priorities, while Track B has explained, rewritten and explored options. The progress strip marks the first three prompts complete and points everyone toward the same sample-file activity.

There's nothing new to send at this checkpoint, so take a moment to reflect on how you checked an answer. For Track A that meant opening work sources; for Track B it meant comparing with supplied facts and examining the reasoning rather than accepting polished wording.
cp1.ask: What did you check on your track before deciding an answer was useful?
cp1.watch: Wait for both tracks to reach the shared checkpoint; explain that prompts 4 and 5 now apply to everyone.

say: Download all three cards: 01_Regional_Resident_Services_Update.docx, 02_Anonymous_Community_Feedback.docx and 03_Regional_Service_Performance.xlsx. Together they provide a weekly service update, anonymous feedback and service-performance figures for the next prompt.

Save them in one folder so you can select the complete set when you start the new chat. These are fictional training samples, not real resident records; using all three lets us compare narrative, feedback and numbers instead of relying on whichever file is easiest to read.
files.ask: Which file would you consult for a performance figure, and which would you consult for a feedback theme?
files.watch: Confirm all three downloads exist before moving on; don't substitute participants' real service or resident files.

say: Both tracks now start a new chat and attach the three sample files before sending this prompt. The animated file chips show the full set; ask for a short service update covering strengths, concerns, feedback themes, missing information and questions to investigate.

Check each finding against the named file, rather than accepting a combined summary because it sounds complete. The request limits the evidence to those attachments, so any unsupported explanation or missing citation is something to challenge, not a gap for us to fill with guesses.
t4do.ask: Can you identify the attached file that supports one concern and one feedback theme?
t4do.watch: Check three attachments before Send for both tracks; if Work IQ is absent, keep learners on the shared file exercise rather than returning to Track A setup.

say: Stay in the same shared file-based chat so the email uses the service update you've just checked. Request a short manager email with the current position, the most urgent concern and three next steps, clearly labelled as recommendations.

Read every figure against the original files and look for language that accidentally turns a proposal into an approved decision. This is a draft for your review, so urgency, facts and suggested action need to remain distinct even when the email is concise and professional.
t5do.ask: Which sentence states a confirmed fact, and which sentence should remain labelled as a recommendation?
t5do.watch: Ensure both tracks use their prompt-4 conversation; allow figure checks before anyone treats the email as ready to send.

say: If time remains, choose one of these four follow-ups in the same chat as your manager-email draft. You can ask for the supporting source, identify missing information, shorten the email for a busy manager or convert the update into briefing points.

Pick the request that addresses a real weakness in your response rather than running all four to finish a list. After the revision, check the evidence again; shortening or reformatting the answer doesn't make an unsupported statement more reliable.
explore.ask: Does your current draft most need a source check, a gap check, shorter wording or briefing points?
explore.watch: Keep this optional and time-bounded; remind learners to stay in the sample-file chat, not their earlier track conversation.

say: The pack collects the five main prompts, Track B's three alternatives and the optional follow-ups, with separate copy buttons where needed. Download copilot-chat-prompts.txt if you'd like the complete sequence for later practice.

When you return to it, choose the opening route that matches your access rather than attempting both tracks as one long workflow. Prompts four and five still belong together around the same three sample files, and the pack doesn't replace checking the responses you get.
pack.ask: Which route and follow-up would you choose if you repeated this workshop without Work IQ?
pack.watch: Point out Track B entries in the pack and the shared file prompts; clarify that downloading prompts does not save the learner's answers.

say: As the recap appears, notice that both tracks led to the same file-review and checked-email skills. You practised starting a useful conversation, working across files, separating facts from recommendations and asking what remains missing.

Choose one of those skills to reuse this week, with a specific source check attached to it. Keep the three habits beside the recap—appropriate information, open the original and decide yourself—and use the journey or Microsoft Learn links when you want to continue.
learned.ask: Which prompt will you reuse this week, and what evidence will you open before acting on its answer?
learned.watch: Invite a brief next-use commitment from either track; don't imply participants all saw the same work-based results.
